abstract: We tackle the online ranking problem of assigning $L$ items to $K$ positions on a web page in order to maximize the number of user clicks. We propose an original algorithm, easy to implement and with strong theoretical guarantees to tackle this problem in the Position-Based Model (PBM) setting, well suited for applications where items are displayed on a grid. Besides learning to rank, our algorithm, GRAB (for parametric Graph for unimodal RAnking Bandit), also learns the parameter of a compact graph over permutations of $K$ items among $L$. The logarithmic regret bound of this algorithm is a direct consequence of the unimodality property of the bandit setting with respect to the learned graph. Experiments against state-of-the-art learning algorithms which also tackle the PBM setting, show that our method is more efficient while giving regret performance on par with the best known algorithms on simulated and real life datasets.

summary.idea: GRAB learns both the ranking and a compact graph connecting item permutations, exploiting a structure in which rewards improve toward a best ranking on that graph.
summary.limitations: The guarantee relies on the position-based model and the associated unimodality property. The abstract does not quantify efficiency gains or evaluate other click-behavior models.
summary.problem: An online ranking system must choose which items occupy limited display positions while learning how those choices affect user clicks.
summary.results: Under the position-based click model, the algorithm has a logarithmic regret bound. Simulated and real-data experiments report greater efficiency with regret comparable to the strongest compared methods.
summary.tldr: Learning a structured graph of rankings enables efficient online item placement with a logarithmic regret guarantee.

title: Parametric Graph for Unimodal Ranking Bandit

abstract: Transformers are slow and memory-hungry on long sequences, since the time and memory complexity of self-attention are quadratic in sequence length. Approximate attention methods have attempted to address this problem by trading off model quality to reduce the compute complexity, but often do not achieve wall-clock speedup. We argue that a missing principle is making attention algorithms IO-aware---accounting for reads and writes between levels of GPU memory. We propose FlashAttention, an IO-aware exact attention algorithm that uses tiling to reduce the number of memory reads/writes between GPU high bandwidth memory (HBM) and GPU on-chip SRAM. We analyze the IO complexity of FlashAttention, showing that it requires fewer HBM accesses than standard attention, and is optimal for a range of SRAM sizes. We also extend FlashAttention, yielding an approximate attention algorithm that is faster than any existing approximate attention method. FlashAttention, 3x speedup on GPT-2 (seq. length 1K), and 2.4x speedup on long-range arena (seq. length 1K-4K). FlashAttention, yielding higher quality models (0.7 better perplexity on GPT-2 and 6.4 points of lift on long-document classification) and entirely new capabilities: the first Transformers to achieve better-than-chance performance on the Path-X challenge (seq. length 16K, 61.4% accuracy) and Path-256 (seq. length 64K, 63.1% accuracy).

summary.idea: FlashAttention computes exact attention in tiles arranged to reduce transfers between high-bandwidth memory and fast on-chip storage. The analysis explicitly accounts for this data movement.
summary.limitations: Exact attention still retains its underlying dense computation. Reported speedups belong to specific sequence lengths and experiments; the abstract does not establish the same gains on every hardware configuration.
summary.problem: Attention can be slow and memory-intensive because it repeatedly transfers large intermediate arrays between GPU memory levels. Reducing arithmetic alone may not improve actual runtime.
summary.results: The abstract reports fewer memory accesses, threefold speedup for the stated GPT-2 setup, and 2.4-fold speedup on Long Range Arena. It also reports improved model evaluations and long-sequence capabilities.
summary.tldr: Speed up exact attention by organizing computation around the GPU's memory hierarchy.

title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness

abstract: This paper explores the realm of infinite horizon average reward Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs). To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to delve into the regret and constraint violation analysis of average reward CMDPs with a general policy parametrization. To address this challenge, we propose a primal dual-based policy gradient algorithm that adeptly manages the constraints while ensuring a low regret guarantee toward achieving a global optimal policy. In particular, our proposed algorithm achieves $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}({T}^{4/5})$ objective regret and $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}({T}^{4/5})$ constraint violation bounds.

summary.idea: The paper proposes a primal-dual policy-gradient algorithm. Policy updates improve reward while dual variables adjust the pressure to satisfy constraints, allowing both objectives to be managed together.
summary.limitations: These are cumulative bounds, so they do not promise zero constraint violations at every step. The abstract does not state all assumptions, empirical evaluations, or the constants governing practical performance.
summary.problem: An agent operating indefinitely may need to maximize long-run average reward while respecting resource or behavior constraints. General policy parameterizations make theoretical performance analysis difficult.
summary.results: The analysis gives objective-regret and constraint-violation bounds scaling as T to the four-fifths, apart from logarithmic factors, for the studied average-reward constrained decision process.
summary.tldr: Analyze reward learning and constraint violations jointly for parameterized policies in continuing decision problems.

title: Learning General Parameterized Policies for Infinite Horizon Average Reward Constrained MDPs via Primal-Dual Policy Gradient Algorithm
